locator: Figure 2, 'Persistent state on all servers' box, p. 4
claim: A Raft server persists currentTerm, votedFor, and its log entries as its persistent state on stable storage.
quote: Persistent state on all servers: (Updated on stable storage before responding to RPCs) currentTerm latest term server has seen (initialized to 0 on first boot, increases monotonically) votedFor candidateId that received vote in current term (or null if none) log[] log entries; each entry contains command for state machine, and term when entry was received by leader (first index is 1)

locator: §3.8 Persisted state and server restarts, p. 27
claim: The commit index needs no persistence because a restarting server can safely reinitialize it to zero.
quote: Other state variables are safe to lose on a restart, as they can all be recreated. The most interesting example is the commit index, which can safely be reinitialized to zero on a restart.

locator: Figure 2, 'Persistent state on all servers' box, p. 4
claim: A server updates its persistent state on stable storage before it responds to any RPC, including RequestVote and AppendEntries.
quote: Persistent state on all servers: (Updated on stable storage before responding to RPCs)

locator: README.md, 'After creating a Node' step 2 (tag v3.7.0)
claim: etcd's raft library requires that no messages be sent until the latest HardState has been persisted to disk.
quote: It is important that no messages be sent until the latest HardState has been persisted to disk, and all Entries written by any previous Ready batch (Messages may be sent while entries from the same batch are being persisted).

locator: §3.8 Persisted state and server restarts, p. 27
claim: Persisting the current term and vote prevents a restarted server from voting twice in the same term.
quote: In particular, each server persists its current term and vote; this is necessary to prevent the server from voting twice in the same term or replacing log entries from a newer leader with those from a deposed leader.

locator: §5.2 Leader election
claim: Raft's majority rule guarantees the Election Safety property: at most one candidate can win the election for a particular term.
quote: The majority rule ensures that at most one candidate can win the election for a particular term (the Election Safety Property in Figure 3).

locator: §3.8 Persisted state and server restarts, p. 27
claim: A server persists new log entries before they are counted toward commitment, which prevents a committed entry from being lost or 'uncommitted' by a restart.
quote: Each server also persists new log entries before they are counted towards the entries’ commitment; this prevents committed entries from being lost or “uncommitted” when servers restart.

locator: §3.6.3 Safety argument, numbered step 4
claim: The Leader Completeness argument relies on the voter that accepted the committed entry still storing it when it later votes for a higher-term leader.
quote: The voter still stored the entry when it voted for leader_U, since every intervening leader contained the entry (by assumption), leaders never remove entries, and followers only remove entries if they conflict with the leader.

quote: They would need to track which servers know of the entry’s commitment, and the servers would need to persist their commit index to disk; neither of these mechanisms is required in Raft.

locator: fsync(2) man page, DESCRIPTION, paragraph on fsync()
claim: fsync blocks until the device reports that the transfer has completed, and this includes writing through or flushing a disk cache if present.
quote: This includes writing through or flushing a disk cache if present.  The call blocks until the device reports that the transfer has completed.

locator: fsync(2) man page, DESCRIPTION, paragraph on directory entries
claim: fsync on a file does not persist the directory entry that names it, so creating a log file needs a separate fsync on the directory.
quote: Calling fsync() does not necessarily ensure that the entry in the directory containing the file has also reached disk.  For that an explicit fsync() on a file descriptor for the directory is also needed.

locator: fsync(2) man page, DESCRIPTION, first paragraph
claim: By specification fsync writes through or flushes a disk cache if one is present, not just the kernel page cache.
quote: This includes writing through or flushing a disk cache if present.

locator: fsync(2) man page, HISTORY, paragraph on fsync() implementations
claim: On older kernels and lesser-used filesystems fsync cannot flush the disk cache, so the disk cache must be disabled for safe operation.
quote: The fsync() implementations in older kernels and lesser used filesystems do not know how to flush disk caches.  In these cases disk caches need to be disabled using hdparm(8) or sdparm(8) to guarantee safe operation.

locator: fsync(2) man page, DESCRIPTION, paragraph on fdatasync()
claim: fdatasync is like fsync but skips flushing metadata that is not needed to read the data back correctly.
quote: fdatasync() is similar to fsync(), but does not flush modified metadata unless that metadata is needed in order to allow a subsequent data retrieval to be correctly handled.

locator: fsync(2) man page, DESCRIPTION, paragraph on fdatasync()
claim: fdatasync still flushes a metadata change such as a file-size change, because that is needed to read the data back.
quote: On the other hand, a change to the file size (st_size, as made by say ftruncate(2)), would require a metadata flush.

locator: README.md, Usage section, responsibility step 2
claim: No Ready messages may be sent until the latest HardState has been persisted to disk and all entries from any previous Ready batch have been written.
quote: It is important that no messages be sent until the latest HardState has been persisted to disk, and all Entries written by any previous Ready batch

locator: section 28.3 Write-Ahead Logging, first paragraph
claim: WAL's defining rule is that changes to the data files must be written only after the changes have been logged and the log records flushed to permanent storage.
quote: Briefly, WAL's central concept is that changes to data files (where tables and indexes reside) must be written only after those changes have been logged, that is, after WAL records describing the changes have been flushed to permanent storage.

locator: section 28.1 Reliability, paragraph on partial disk-platter writes
claim: PostgreSQL periodically writes full page images to the WAL before modifying the page on disk, so crash recovery can restore partially written pages from the WAL.
quote: To guard against such failures, PostgreSQL periodically writes full page images to permanent WAL storage *before* modifying the actual page on disk. By doing this, during crash recovery PostgreSQL can restore partially-written pages from WAL.

locator: section 28.1 Reliability, bulleted list of storage protections, first bullet
claim: Every WAL record carries a CRC-32C checksum that is checked during crash recovery, so an incompletely or incorrectly written record can be detected instead of being replayed as if it were complete.
quote: Each individual record in a WAL file is protected by a CRC-32C (32-bit) check that allows us to tell if record contents are correct. The CRC value is set when we write each WAL record and checked during crash recovery, archive recovery and replication.

locator: section 3.8 Persisted state and server restarts
claim: After a restart a persistent Raft state machine has already applied most log entries, so the last applied index must be persisted to avoid applying those entries a second time.
quote: A persistent state machine, however, has already applied most entries after a restart; to avoid reapplying them, its last applied index must also be persistent.

locator: section 12 Attributes of ARIES, item (4)
claim: ARIES makes redo idempotent by consulting the LSN stored on each page to decide whether a logged operation still needs to be redone.
quote: Idempotence of operations is ensured since the LSN on each page is used to determine whether an operation should be redone or not.

locator: section 28.3 Write-Ahead Logging, third paragraph
claim: Only the WAL file must be flushed to disk to make a transaction durable, rather than every data file the transaction changed, which is why commit can sync the WAL alone.
quote: Using WAL results in a significantly reduced number of disk writes, because only the WAL file needs to be flushed to disk to guarantee that a transaction is committed, rather than every data file changed by the transaction.

locator: section 2 Hardware Assumptions
claim: SQLite's atomic-commit procedure assumes a sector write may be interrupted part-way so that only a portion of the sector is changed, though the write is assumed to run linearly from one end of the sector.
quote: SQLite has traditionally assumed that a sector write is not atomic. However, SQLite does always assume that a sector write is linear.

locator: section 2 Hardware Assumptions, paragraph on the VFS xDeviceCharacteristics method
claim: A VFS may declare that sector writes are atomic, in which case SQLite exploits it, but the default Unix and Windows VFSes do not, so SQLite normally assumes non-atomic sector writes.
quote: The xDeviceCharacteristics method might indicate that sector writes are atomic, and if it does so indicate, SQLite will try to take advantage of that fact. But the default xDeviceCharacteristics method for both Unix and Windows does not indicate atomic sector writes and so these optimizations are normally omitted.

locator: README.md, Usage, step 1
claim: The application must write Entries, then HardState and Snapshot, to persistent storage in that order, or write them together if the storage supports atomic writes.
quote: Write Entries, HardState and Snapshot to persistent storage in order, i.e. Entries first, then HardState and Snapshot if they are not empty. If persistent storage supports atomic writes then all of them can be written together.

locator: FAQ, Deployment, "Why an odd number of cluster members?"
claim: Quorum for n etcd members is (n/2)+1, and because adding a node to an odd-sized cluster always increases the quorum, an odd-sized cluster is preferred.
quote: An etcd cluster needs a majority of nodes, a quorum, to agree on updates to the cluster state. For a cluster with n members, quorum is (n/2)+1. For any odd-sized cluster, adding one node will always increase the number of nodes necessary for quorum.

locator: FAQ, Deployment, "What is maximum cluster size?"
claim: etcd has no hard theoretical cluster-size limit, but a cluster probably should have no more than seven nodes.
quote: Theoretically, there is no hard limit. However, an etcd cluster probably should have no more than seven nodes.

locator: README.md, Implementation notes (repeated in doc.go, Implementation notes)
claim: Because removing a member from a two-member cluster can leave it unable to make progress, the etcd Raft library recommends using three or more nodes in every cluster.
quote: This approach introduces a problem when removing a member from a two-member cluster: If one of the members dies before the other one receives the commit of the confchange entry, then the member cannot be removed any more since the cluster cannot make progress. For this reason it is highly recommended to use three or more nodes in every cluster.

locator: section 3.5 Creating A Rollback Journal File
claim: SQLite writes the original content of the database pages it is about to change into a rollback journal before modifying them, so the journal holds everything needed to restore the database to its original state.
quote: Prior to making any changes to the database file, SQLite first creates a separate rollback journal file and writes into the rollback journal the original content of the database pages that are to be altered. The idea behind the rollback journal is that it contains all information needed to restore the database back to its original state.
